title: Clean Romance Books Like Bridgerton | Regency Reads Without the Steam
kicker: A reading guide, written with a raised eyebrow
desc: Loved the ballrooms, dukes and gossip of Bridgerton but want your romance closed-door? A witty guide to clean Regency romance books like Bridgerton, with where to start.
lead: So. You have finished the latest season, wept discreetly into a cushion, and now find yourself staring at the wall with the hollow look of a debutante whose dance card has gone mysteriously blank. You want more ballrooms. You want more dukes who are far too pleased with themselves. You would like, if it is not too much trouble, rather fewer scenes that require you to angle your telephone away from your mother. Dear reader, you have come to exactly the right drawing room.
gossip: It has come to the attention of this column that a great many ladies of excellent taste have been seen pressing their noses to the window of the clean romance shop. One lady was overheard to declare that she adores a smouldering duke but cannot abide being made to blush on public transport. Another confessed she would happily read the slow burn of a glance across a ballroom for three hundred pages, provided the duke eventually does something about it. We are pleased to report that he does. Eventually. It is the eventually that is the fun.
books_heading: Where to begin, if you are the sort who likes a ballroom

books.why: It opens with a public jilting in a ballroom full of three hundred witnesses, a glass of champagne, and a heroine who discovers that her first feeling is fury rather than heartbreak. Then she is packed off to a remote estate with a duke who has stopped letting anyone look at him. If you loved a slow, stubborn courtship between two people who are each convinced they are unlovable, begin here.

A grumpy duke, a widow who has run entirely out of patience, and a great deal of arguing across breakfast tables. If your favourite thing in the world is two people who insist they cannot stand each other while plainly standing each other very well indeed, this is your book.
A shorter read with a reformed rake, one inn, one bed, and a snowstorm with no sense of decorum. Perfect for a single evening and a pot of tea you will forget to drink.

quotes.text: Was the gown intended as a parting gift? Or merely the costume for this particular performance?
I should hate to deprive them. It is the best entertainment Lady Castleton has provided all season, and the orchestra has not even resumed.
quotes.who: Ariana again, who will not be made small

checklist_heading: You may be in a Bridgerton sort of mood if
checklist: You have opinions about which sibling deserves the next season
The phrase “marriage mart” makes your pulse quicken
You find a man glowering at a pianoforte inexplicably attractive
You have, at least once, sighed at the kettle as though it were a duke
You would like the kissing, the longing and the happily-ever-after, with the bedroom door politely shut

sections.h2: What we adore about Bridgerton, in no particular order
paras: It is the world, mostly. The marriage mart with its rules and its quiet cruelties. The mothers who scheme with the precision of field marshals. The scandal sheet that can ruin a girl before she has finished her chocolate. And the strange, thrilling freedom of two people who may only speak honestly when nobody else is listening, which in Regency London is roughly once a fortnight and usually behind a potted palm.

The romance works because the rules are so very tight. A glance across a ballroom is a declaration when a glance is all anyone is permitted. A gloved hand held one moment too long is practically an elopement. Nobody in 1813 could text, which is a great mercy for the novelist and a great inconvenience for the heroine.

sections.h2: Then there are the dukes
paras: Dukes, viscounts, and the occasional rake who has been running from something for years and is at last run to ground by a woman with better aim. Readers return again and again for the moment such a man realises that the lady before him has seen straight through his armour, has found it poorly made, and is not in the least impressed.

Mothers of the ton will tell you that a duke is the highest prize of the season. Readers of romance know better. The prize is the duke who has been brought, quite against his will, to say something sincere.

sections.h2: Why some of us prefer the clean version
paras: Julia Quinn's novels and the Netflix series both include open-door love scenes, and plenty of readers enjoy them enormously. Plenty of others would rather skip ahead, read on the train without a strategic tilt of the screen, or pass a book to a mother, a daughter or a book club without first issuing a stern warning. Clean Regency romance keeps the ballrooms, the banter and the yearning, and leaves the bedroom door firmly shut.

Clean does not mean dull, whatever certain gentlemen at the club may say. The tension in a closed-door book must come from somewhere, so it comes from the arrangement that cannot be broken, the conversation interrupted for the fourth time by an aunt, and the duke who notices how a lady takes her tea and is appalled at himself for noticing. Many readers find that slow burn more romantic, since the waiting is half the pleasure and the other half is watching him suffer.

sections.h2: How to spot a proper clean read-alike
paras: Look for a Regency or late Georgian setting, somewhere between 1795 and 1837, with a season, a country house or two, and a very firm idea of what is proper. Add a hero with a title and an excellent reason to keep everyone at arm's length. Add a heroine with something to lose, be it her reputation, her income or her family's good name. Stir in a trope with built-in trouble, such as a marriage of convenience, a fake engagement or two enemies obliged to share a carriage. Finish with a happily-ever-after, because nobody reads this genre to be left sobbing in a hedge.
On the cover or in the blurb, the magic words are clean, sweet, closed-door or fade-to-black. All four mean the romance stays on the page and the rest happens tactfully offstage.

sections.h2: Other clean Regency authors for your shelf
paras: If you mean to furnish an entire library, Georgette Heyer more or less invented the Regency romance and remains wickedly funny and entirely clean. Julie Klassen writes longer, atmospheric historical novels with a gentle thread of faith. Sarah M. Eden and Martha Keyes both write sweet Regency series with large families you can follow from book to book, which is the next best thing to having siblings who meddle on your behalf. Emma's books sit happily alongside them, with a little more heartache and heroes who have been through the wars, occasionally literally.

faq.q: Are the Bridgerton books clean?
faq.a: No. Julia Quinn's Bridgerton novels include open-door love scenes, as does the Netflix series. Clean Regency romance keeps a similar setting and the same sparkle, with the intimacy kept tactfully off the page.

faq.q: What does closed-door romance mean?
faq.a: A closed-door romance has kissing and a great deal of romantic tension, but any love scenes happen off the page. The story bows out at the bedroom door and comes back in the morning looking innocent.

faq.q: Which Emma Velott book should I read first if I liked Bridgerton?
faq.a: A Jilted Bride for the Battle-Scarred Duke. It opens at a society ball with a spectacular public jilting and becomes a slow-burn romance with a reclusive duke. You can read the prologue free on this site.

faq.q: Do I need to read Emma's books in order?
faq.a: Not at all. Each book is a standalone with its own couple and a complete happily-ever-after.

title: Marriage of Convenience Regency Romance Books (Clean) | Emma Velott
kicker: A reading guide for the sensibly wed
desc: Clean marriage of convenience Regency romance books, from arranged matches to fake marriages. A witty guide to why readers love the trope, and where to start with Emma Velott.
lead: Two people marry for every reason in the world except love. A debt. A scandal. An heir. A roof. A particularly persistent mother. They sign the register, shake hands like bankers, and agree to separate bedchambers and civil breakfasts. Then they have to actually live together, and the arrangement that looked so very sensible on paper begins, slowly and delightfully, to fall to pieces.
gossip: We hear that a certain duke has married his housekeeper, or very nearly, and that the household is divided on whether this was a matter of convenience or of temper. The footmen insist the new duchess frightens His Grace. The maids insist His Grace has never looked better. The cook, consulted privately, said only that the breakfast trays are coming back empty for the first time in years, and drew her own conclusions.
books_heading: Marriages made in haste, by Emma Velott

books.why: A widow takes a housekeeping post with a duke who has emptied his own house of servants, and what begins as a trial becomes an arrangement, and the arrangement becomes a marriage neither of them meant to want. Grumpy hero, outspoken heroine, a secret that will not stay buried.

The fake-marriage version, for those who like their vows entirely invented. A governess and a rake pose as husband and wife at a snowbound inn to save her reputation, with strict rules about which side of the bed is whose. The rules are broken almost at once.
Not a marriage of convenience at the start, but made of the same slow, reluctant closeness, as a jilted bride takes a position in a reclusive duke's household and declines to pretend he is furniture.

quotes.text: And how long have we been married, Mrs. Cathcart? These details matter. The innkeeper’s wife will ask. Innkeepers’ wives always ask.
I am incapable of mild attachment. It is a defect of the bloodline.
quotes.who: Simon, who was asked to be mildly attached

checklist_heading: Signs you are in a marriage of convenience romance
checklist: Someone has used the word “arrangement” with a perfectly straight face
There is a contract, and it has a clause about bedchambers
One of them is pretending very hard not to notice how the other takes their tea
A dinner guest asks how they met, and they give two different answers
By chapter twenty the arrangement is in tatters and nobody is sorry

sections.h2: Why the trope fits the Regency like a good glove
paras: In 1815, marriage really was a practical affair. A lady had very few ways to keep herself, estates required heirs, debts required paying, and a single rumour could close every door in Mayfair before luncheon. A sensible match was perfectly ordinary, which means the trope never feels forced in a Regency setting. Our couple are simply doing what everyone around them does, only rather worse at it.

The romance lives in the gap between the contract and the people. They agreed to separate rooms and polite conversation. Nobody agreed to notice the way the other laughs at the newspaper, or to lie awake when they come home late, or to feel that small, alarming jolt when a sleeve brushes a sleeve on the stairs. That was never in the paperwork.

sections.h2: A field guide to the varieties
paras: The arranged match is settled by families or circumstance before the couple have much say, and usually over their strenuous objections. The marriage of convenience proper is chosen by the couple themselves, generally because each has something the other needs and neither will admit to anything else. The fake marriage is a performance for the outside world, with the added peril of being found out by an innkeeper's wife. The compromised marriage happens when the couple are discovered in a library, a garden or a snowdrift, and society can think of no other answer.

Each one produces the same delicious problem. The couple are bound together long before they trust each other, and the whole of the book is spent closing that distance one awkward breakfast at a time.

sections.h2: What makes a clean marriage of convenience sing
paras: In a closed-door book the wedding night is not the turning point, so the emotional milestones must carry all the weight. The first real conversation. The first time one of them defends the other in public, loudly and to the astonishment of a viscountess. The moment one realises the other has been quietly kind for weeks and never said a word about it. Lovers of this trope tend to cherish the in-between scenes, the shared suppers and the letters and the evenings by the fire, more than any grand declaration.
Emma writes these marriages slowly on purpose, so that when the happily-ever-after arrives it has been properly earned and not merely signed for.

faq.q: What is a marriage of convenience romance?
faq.a: A romance in which the couple marry for practical reasons, such as money, reputation or an heir, and then have the great inconvenience of falling in love. It is one of the most beloved tropes in historical romance.

faq.q: Are Emma Velott's marriage of convenience books clean?
faq.a: Yes. Every one of Emma's books is a clean, closed-door Regency romance with a happily-ever-after.

faq.q: What is the difference between a fake marriage and a marriage of convenience?
faq.a: In a marriage of convenience the couple are truly wed. In a fake marriage they only pretend to be, which adds the delightful risk of discovery. The Rakish Viscount's Pretend Wife is a fake marriage story.

title: Scarred Hero Romance Books | Clean Wounded Duke Regency Romance
kicker: A reading guide for the tender-hearted
desc: Clean scarred hero and wounded duke Regency romance. Battle-scarred dukes, reclusive heroes and the heroines who refuse to look away. Where to start with Emma Velott.
lead: He came home from the war with a face he no longer shows anyone, or a wound nobody can see. He has shut up the house, banished the mirrors, and given himself a list of rules that would make a monastery blush. Then a woman arrives who will not keep to the rooms she has been given, and who will not pretend she has not noticed him. Readers come back to the scarred hero again and again, and it is easy to see why.
gossip: Word reaches this column of a certain duke who has not received a caller in four years and is said to keep four rules, the last of which concerns mirrors. Word also reaches us of a young lady, lately and very publicly jilted, who has taken a position under his roof as companion to his sister. The village is agog. The sister is delighted. The duke himself has not yet been consulted, which we suspect is precisely how the young lady prefers it.

books.why: Ronan Kingsford, sixth Duke of Penwythe, came back from the war with a hand that will not close and has not let anyone past his gates in four years. Ariana, freshly jilted before three hundred guests, has her own reasons for avoiding being looked at. A slow, tender romance in the grand tradition of Beauty and the Beast, with rather more sarcasm.
Here the wounds are the hidden sort. A duke who has emptied his own house, and a widow who sees, before anybody else, that his coldness is only armour.

quotes.text: I will not be made small again.
You are leaving the room without standing up. It is a newer trick and I do not care for it.
quotes.who: An old friend, to a duke who has stopped letting anyone in

checklist_heading: You may be in a scarred hero romance if
checklist: An entire wing of the house is shut up and nobody will say why
The hero has rules, and one of them concerns mirrors
The servants speak of him in the tone usually reserved for weather
The heroine walks straight past the rules on her first morning
Somebody, at some point, takes his scarred hand and does not let go

sections.h2: Why we cannot resist a scarred hero
paras: The scarred hero is a man who has decided he is unlovable and then arranged his entire life, his house, his servants and his breakfast hour around that conclusion. The romance is the slow, glorious dismantling of it. He expects pity or revulsion and receives neither. He expects her to leave and she stays, mostly out of stubbornness. Every small act of ordinary attention lands harder because he had stopped expecting any at all.

It is also a trope about seeing clearly. The heroine is usually the first person in years to look at him properly, scars and temper and terrible manners included, and decide he is worth the trouble. A great many readers find that more romantic than any quantity of flawless cheekbones.

sections.h2: Battle scars and the Regency
paras: The Regency sits at the very end of the Napoleonic Wars, which finished at Waterloo in 1815. Thousands of officers came home changed, and a good number of them were heirs to great estates. That history gives the wounded duke a real foundation. His retreat from the ballroom makes sense, and so does his horror of being stared at by the same people who once begged him to dance.
Hidden wounds serve just as well. Grief, guilt, a betrayal that taught him to keep the door locked. The scar need not be on his face for the story to break your heart a little before mending it.

sections.h2: The heroine who simply will not look away
paras: The best scarred-hero heroines are neither nurses nor saints. They are women with troubles of their own who happen to be kind, or stubborn, or simply too tired to be frightened of him. Ariana in A Jilted Bride has just been humiliated before the whole of society, and she recognises a fellow hider the moment she sets eyes on one. Their story is about two people who have both been looked at the wrong way learning, with enormous reluctance, to be looked at the right one.

faq.q: What is a scarred hero romance?
faq.a: A romance in which the hero carries a physical or emotional wound, often from war, that has driven him to withdraw from the world. The heroine draws him back out, usually without asking his permission.

faq.q: Is A Jilted Bride for the Battle-Scarred Duke a Beauty and the Beast retelling?
faq.a: It shares the shape, with a reclusive scarred duke in a remote house and a heroine who refuses to be frightened of him, but it is an original clean Regency romance.

faq.q: Are these books clean?
faq.a: Yes. Emma's scarred hero romances are closed-door, with a happily-ever-after.

title: Grumpy Duke Romance Books | Clean Grumpy Sunshine Regency Romance
kicker: A reading guide, served with a scowl
desc: Clean grumpy duke romance, where a cold, scowling duke meets a heroine who refuses to be frightened of him. Witty grumpy sunshine Regency romance by Emma Velott.
lead: He scowls. He dismisses footmen with a look. He has a reputation in three counties for being quite impossible and appears to have worked very hard for it. And then a woman walks into his house who simply does not care, and tells him so. The grumpy duke is one of the most satisfying heroes in all of Regency romance, chiefly because of what happens when he finally, grudgingly, softens.
gossip: This column is reliably informed that the Duke of Wrenwick has gone through more servants than most gentlemen go through cravats. His table is laid every morning for a man who never sits at it. His footmen pour with trembling hands. We are now told that a widow of no particular fortune has accepted the post of housekeeper at twice the going rate and lasted three entire days before informing His Grace that fear is a very expensive economy. Wagers at the gentlemen's clubs are running heavily in her favour.

books.why: The Duke of Wrenwick has frightened off every servant he ever employed. Anastasia lasts three days before telling him precisely what his temper costs him. The grumpiest duke on Emma's shelf, and the most satisfying to watch unravel.
Ronan is less cross and more withdrawn, a duke who would very much like everyone to go away. For readers who prefer their grumpy hero wounded underneath.

quotes.text: I asked for a housekeeper, not a humorist.
You are merely stubborn, and you have dressed it in better tailoring than most men can afford for their virtues.
quotes.who: An old friend, to a cold duke

checklist_heading: The grumpy duke, a brief diagnostic
checklist: Has not smiled in public since approximately 1809
Eats breakfast alone, with the newspaper held up like a shield
Insists he does not care, then does something enormously caring by accident
Is undone, at last, by a woman who argues back
Pretends the gift he bought her was an oversight

sections.h2: Why readers adore a grumpy hero
paras: A grumpy hero is a promise. Somewhere beneath all that scowling lives a man who cares a great deal and has decided it is far safer not to show it, and the story will, in time, prove it beyond all doubt. Readers relish the sparring on the way there, and they relish even more the small cracks, such as the first reluctant smile, the gift he insists was a mistake, and the moment he loses his temper on her behalf instead of at her.

Make him a duke and you add power to the mixture. He is accustomed to being obeyed by everyone from his valet to the House of Lords. A heroine who will not obey him, and who has excellent reasons, unsettles his entire world in a way that is tremendously enjoyable to read.

sections.h2: Grumpy and sunshine, or grumpy and fire
paras: The classic pairing is grumpy and sunshine, a sour hero and a warm, hopeful heroine who wins him over with kindness and a suspicious quantity of baked goods. Emma tends to write the other version, in which the heroine has a temper of her own and has run entirely out of patience for powerful men who behave badly. Both work beautifully. The sunshine heroine wins him with warmth and the fiery heroine wins him by refusing to back down, and in either case he never quite recovers, nor wishes to.

sections.h2: What separates a grumpy duke from a merely rude one
paras: A grumpy hero requires a reason. Grief, a betrayal, a responsibility shouldered far too young. Without one he is simply ill-mannered, and nobody wishes to marry a man who is merely ill-mannered, whatever his rent roll. The finest grumpy dukes are cold to the world and quietly decent in private, and the heroine is the first to notice the difference. In a clean romance, that slow reveal carries the whole story, so every softened word counts double.

faq.q: What is a grumpy duke romance?
faq.a: A historical romance in which the hero is a cold, short-tempered or forbidding duke who is gradually, and very much against his will, won over by the heroine. It is often paired with the grumpy sunshine trope.

faq.q: Which Emma Velott book has the grumpiest duke?
faq.a: A Fiery Widow for the Cold Duke. By the time the heroine arrives, the Duke of Wrenwick has emptied his own house of staff.

faq.q: Are Emma Velott's books clean?
faq.a: Yes. They are closed-door Regency romances with a happily-ever-after.

title: Sweet Historical Romance Books (Clean Regency) | Emma Velott
kicker: A reading guide for the delicately inclined
desc: What sweet and clean historical romance means, how it differs from closed-door and steamy romance, and the best clean Regency romance books to start with. A witty guide.
lead: Sweet, clean, closed-door, fade-to-black. Readers and booksellers bandy these words about with the confidence of chaperones, and they do not always mean quite the same thing. What follows is a plain guide to what each one means in historical romance, offered in the spirit of a kindly aunt who would rather you did not open the wrong book on the omnibus.
gossip: A lady of our acquaintance reports that she once purchased a novel described as “sweet” and was obliged to read chapter fourteen with a cushion over the page. She has since become a devoted student of the heat-level label and urges all her friends to do likewise. We share her guidance below, in the hope of sparing other ladies the cushion.
books_heading: Clean Regency romances by Emma Velott

books.why: A slow-burn, emotional romance with a scarred duke. Longing, kisses, a great deal of tension, and nothing that requires a cushion.
A grumpy duke, a widow, a marriage of convenience and a good deal of sparring. Closed-door.
A light, funny novella about a fake marriage at a snowbound inn. They share a bed and keep, more or less, to their own sides of it.

quotes.text: Married four hours, and already she knows me better than my own mother.
You were unconscious, sir. I prodded you with my elbow and you said, and I quote, mmrph.

checklist_heading: The heat-level guide, for the cautious reader
checklist: Sweet means kisses only, and the language would not alarm a curate
Clean means nothing explicit on the page, though married couples are permitted to be married
Closed-door means the story bows out at the bedroom door and returns the next morning
Fade-to-black means much the same as closed-door, with a more theatrical name
Steamy means you will want the cushion

sections.h2: Sweet, clean and closed-door, explained without blushing
paras: Sweet romance usually means kisses only, with no love scenes on or off the page and language mild enough for a vicarage tea. Clean romance is close cousin to sweet and is the word most readers search for. Closed-door means the couple may well have a wedding night, but the narrative retires at the bedroom door with perfect discretion and rejoins them at breakfast. Fade-to-black is simply closed-door in a more dramatic hat.

Emma's books are clean and closed-door. There is longing in abundance, there are kisses worth waiting for, and married couples are allowed to be married, but nothing explicit appears on the page and the language stays gentle enough to read aloud to an aunt.

sections.h2: Why so many readers choose clean historical romance
paras: Some readers simply prefer it. Others want books they can share with mothers and daughters, read on the morning commute, or recommend to a book club without a hurried disclaimer. A great many say the slow build of a clean romance is the more satisfying, since every touch matters enormously when there are so very few of them.

The Regency is especially well suited to the clean romance. Its manners were strict to the point of comedy, a couple might go weeks without five unchaperoned minutes together, and a waltz or a turn about the garden could carry the weight of a proposal. The period does half the work of building tension, and the author need only keep the aunts out of the way.

sections.h2: Beloved tropes in sweet historical romance
paras: Marriage of convenience, fake engagement, the reformed rake, the wounded or grumpy duke, the governess or companion in a great house, enemies to lovers, and two people trapped together by weather are all perennial favourites. You will find a good many of them in Emma's books, and each has its own reading guide on this site, should you wish to indulge.

faq.q: What is the difference between sweet and clean romance?
faq.a: The two overlap a great deal. Sweet romance usually means kisses only, while clean romance may include married intimacy as long as it happens off the page. Neither includes explicit scenes.

faq.q: Are Emma Velott's books sweet or clean?
faq.a: Clean and closed-door. There are kisses and plenty of romantic tension, and anything more happens off the page.

faq.q: Where can I buy Emma Velott's books?
faq.a: Directly from this website as EPUB and PDF ebooks that work on any device, or on Kobo.

desc: Read every Georgette Heyer and want more? Clean, witty Regency romance books like Georgette Heyer, with sparkling banter, managing heroines and dukes who meet their match.
lead: You have read Frederica on a rainy weekend and The Grand Sophy on a sunny one. You have quoted Venetia at people who did not deserve it. You know your phaeton from your curricle and you have, at least once, called a perfectly modern gentleman a care-for-nobody to his face. And now, alas, you have come to the end of the shelf. Pray do not despair. The Regency is a large country and there are still a great many houses left to visit.

Her family are concerned. Her neighbours are entertained. She has asked this column whether there is anything else in the world that sparkles quite the same way, and we have taken the liberty of answering below.

books.why: A managing heroine who walks into a duke's household and sets about rearranging it, and him, with a ruthless eye. Heyer readers who loved a capable woman taking charge of a hopeless gentleman will feel at home here.
Quick, quarrelsome banter between a prim governess and a rake who refuses to take anything seriously. If the comic sparring was your favourite part of Heyer, start here.

A heroine who meets public humiliation with a raised chin and a very sharp tongue, and a duke who has hidden himself away. A little more heartache than Heyer usually allows, with the same refusal to be made small.

quotes.text: You have had victims. There is a difference, and it is chiefly that the victims left.
quotes.who: A frank friend, on a duke's former housekeepers

quotes.text: You will discover the rules as you break them. It appears to be the only pace at which you learn.
quotes.who: Delilah Pearce, laying down the law

checklist_heading: You may be a confirmed Heyer reader if
checklist: You can tell a high-perch phaeton from a gig at fifty paces
You think a hero who says very little and notices everything is the height of romance
You have strong feelings about the correct way to tie a cravat

sections.h2: What makes Georgette Heyer so very hard to replace
paras: Georgette Heyer more or less invented the Regency romance as we know it, and she did it with an almost unfair amount of style. Her novels are clean, very funny and crammed with period detail, from the slang of the day to the exact cut of a coat. Her heroines are clever and frequently ungovernable. Her heroes range from the brusque and taciturn to the languid and devastatingly well dressed, and readers have argued happily for decades over which kind is best.

Above all, Heyer romances are made of talk. Couples fall in love through quarrels, schemes, misunderstandings and a great deal of wit, and the kissing tends to arrive late and briefly. That is precisely why her books feel so romantic. Every exchange is a duel, and the reader is the only one who can see who is winning.

sections.h2: What to look for in a book like Heyer
paras: Look first for the voice. A good Heyer read-alike is witty in the narration as well as in the dialogue, and it trusts the reader to enjoy a long, elegant quarrel. Look next for the heroine, who should be capable, opinionated and quite unwilling to faint. Then look for the setting, which should be the real Regency, with its rules and its absurdities treated as both a stage and a joke.
Finally, check the heat level. Heyer is clean, and many modern Regency novels are not. Words like clean, sweet or closed-door in the description will keep you safe from unwelcome surprises.

sections.h2: Other authors Heyer readers love
paras: Jane Austen is the obvious companion, and many Heyer devotees came to her by way of Pride and Prejudice. For modern clean Regency romance, Julianne Donaldson's Edenbrooke is a much-loved standalone with a lively heroine, and Sarah M. Eden, Martha Keyes and Josi S. Kilpack all write sweet Regency stories with plenty of humour. Emma's own books lean into the same quarrelsome banter, with heroes who have been through rather more than a lost wager.

faq.q: Are Georgette Heyer's books clean?
faq.a: Yes. Georgette Heyer's Regency romances are clean, with romance conveyed through wit and dialogue and no explicit scenes.

faq.q: Which Georgette Heyer book should I read first?
faq.a: Readers most often recommend Frederica, The Grand Sophy, Venetia or Cotillion as starting points. All are standalone Regency romances.

faq.q: Which Emma Velott book is most like Georgette Heyer?
faq.a: The Rakish Viscount's Pretend Wife has the quickest comic banter, and A Fiery Widow for the Cold Duke has the most Heyer-like managing heroine.

title: Books for Jane Austen Lovers | Clean Regency Romance Like Pride and Prejudice
kicker: A reading guide for those who have rewatched the lake scene
desc: Clean romance books for Jane Austen lovers, with the wit of Pride and Prejudice and the longing of Persuasion. Regency romance like Jane Austen, and where to start.
lead: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a reader in possession of a well-thumbed Pride and Prejudice must be in want of something else to read. You have met Mr. Darcy in every adaptation. You have sighed over Captain Wentworth's letter more times than is strictly healthy. You have even, in a weak moment, given Mansfield Park a second chance. Now you would like something new that still feels like candlelight and good manners and a man who is slower than he ought to be to say what he means.
gossip: This column has learned of a book club in a quiet market town that has read Pride and Prejudice six years running and come to blows, very politely, over whether the 1995 or the 2005 Mr. Darcy is superior. A truce has been proposed. Its terms require each member to bring a new Regency romance to the next meeting, and the club secretary has asked us, rather desperately, for suggestions.

books.why: A heroine who meets humiliation with wit and a duke whose pride and pain keep him at a distance. Austen readers who love a slow change of heart, and a man who must learn to be seen, will find a great deal here.
Two people with fixed first impressions of each other, both wrong, slowly put right across a great many breakfasts. A clean romance of manners with a sharp tongue.
A light, comic novella with a sensible heroine and a gentleman of no sense whatsoever. For readers whose favourite Austen scenes are the funny ones.

checklist_heading: You may be an incurable Austen reader if
checklist: You have taken a long walk purely in the hope of something happening

sections.h2: Why Austen readers are so hard to please
paras: Jane Austen wrote during the Regency itself, so her novels are not historical romance at all but sharp, funny portraits of her own world. That gives them an ease and an irony no modern writer can quite copy. Her heroines are clever, her villains are charming, and her love stories turn on character, on pride and prejudice and persuasion, rather than on grand gestures. The romance arrives late and quietly and lands like a thunderclap.
Austen is also, of course, entirely clean. Her couples rarely so much as kiss on the page, and the longing is all the stronger for it.

sections.h2: What to look for in a book like Austen
paras: Look for a heroine with a mind of her own and a social position that makes it awkward to use. Look for a hero whose first impression is wrong in some important way. Look for wit in the narration, a world full of rules, and a love story that grows out of conversation and misunderstanding. Regency romance is the natural next step, since it is set in Austen's own period and borrows a good deal of her furniture.
Many modern Regency romances are steamier than Austen ever was, so if you prefer her restraint, look for the words clean, sweet or closed-door.

sections.h2: Other authors Austen lovers adore
paras: Georgette Heyer is the classic next step, with all of Austen's wit and rather more slang. Julianne Donaldson's Edenbrooke is a modern clean favourite that many Austen readers recommend to one another, and Sarah M. Eden and Martha Keyes write sweet Regency romance with the same gentle comedy of manners. Emma's books sit among them, with a little more heartache and heroes who have earned their brooding.

faq.q: What should I read after Pride and Prejudice?
faq.a: Many readers move on to Austen's Persuasion and Emma, then to Georgette Heyer and to clean modern Regency romance, which keeps Austen's setting and restraint.

faq.q: Is Regency romance the same as Jane Austen?
faq.a: Not quite. Austen wrote about her own time. Regency romance is written later and set in that same period, usually with the romance placed front and centre.

faq.q: Are Emma Velott's books clean like Austen?
faq.a: Yes. Emma writes clean, closed-door Regency romance with a happily-ever-after.

title: Clean Authors Like Julia Quinn | Witty Regency Romance Without the Steam
kicker: A reading guide for lovers of large families and larger quarrels
desc: Love Julia Quinn's humour, families and banter but want a clean read? Witty, closed-door Regency romance authors like Julia Quinn, and where to start with Emma Velott.
lead: Julia Quinn writes the kind of Regency romance that makes you laugh out loud on a train and then pretend you were coughing. The siblings bicker, the mothers scheme, the heroines are quick and the heroes are undone. If there is a complaint to be made, it is only that some readers would prefer to skip certain chapters, and are tired of skipping. This guide is for those readers, offered with every respect to the lady herself.
gossip: A gentleman of our acquaintance has confessed, under some duress, that he reads his wife's Regency romances when she is out, and that his favourite parts are the arguments. He was very particular that we should not print his name. We are only too happy to oblige, and to recommend to him, and to his wife, a few books with all of the arguments and none of the blushing.
books_heading: Emma's books for Julia Quinn fans

books.why: The funniest of Emma's books, all quick banter and inventive lying to an innkeeper. If you love a Quinn hero who talks too much and a heroine who talks back, this is the one.
A grumpy duke, a heroine with a temper, and household chaos at every turn. Sharp dialogue and a satisfying thaw.
A ballroom scandal, a quick-tongued heroine and a reclusive duke, and a young sister who needs a companion far more than her brother would admit.

sections.h2: What we love about Julia Quinn
paras: Julia Quinn's Bridgerton books made the Regency feel like a family dinner at which everyone is a little too clever. Her romances are built on comedy, on warm, noisy families, and on dialogue that moves so quickly you hardly notice the plot. Her heroes are often far less in control than they think, and her heroines are delighted to point this out.
Her books do include open-door love scenes, which plenty of readers enjoy. Plenty of others love everything else about them and would happily trade those chapters for a few more arguments.

sections.h2: Finding the same sparkle in a clean book
paras: Look for an author whose blurbs make you smile. Comedy is harder to fake than heat, so a funny description is a good sign. Look for families and friendships around the couple, for a heroine who argues, and for dialogue on every page of the sample. Then check the heat level, and choose books labelled clean, sweet or closed-door.
Reading a free first chapter is the quickest test of all. If the first page makes you laugh, the rest probably will.

sections.h2: Other clean authors Quinn readers enjoy
paras: Georgette Heyer is the grandmother of the witty Regency romance and is entirely clean. Julianne Donaldson's Edenbrooke has the playful heroine and the swoon. Sarah M. Eden, Martha Keyes and Josi S. Kilpack write sweet Regency series full of siblings and friends. Emma's books bring the quarrelling, the scheming relatives and the happily-ever-after, with the door kept shut.

faq.q: Are Julia Quinn's books clean?
faq.a: No. Julia Quinn's Regency romances, including the Bridgerton series, include open-door love scenes.

faq.q: Who writes clean books like Julia Quinn?
faq.a: Readers often suggest Georgette Heyer, Julianne Donaldson, Sarah M. Eden and Martha Keyes, and Emma Velott writes witty clean Regency romance in the same spirit.

faq.q: Can I read a sample before buying Emma's books?
faq.a: Yes. Every book on this site has its first chapter or prologue free to read.
